TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.question: How are the annual gas savings calculated when replacing a high-bleed pneumatic controller with a low-bleed one?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.answer: Annual gas savings equal the difference in annual bleed rates between the replaced high-bleed controller and the new low-bleed device, assuming 8,760 hours of operation, multiplied by the gas price.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.evidence: The annual gas savings are equal to the difference in the annual bleed rates between the replaced high-bleed controller and the new low-bleed device (assuming 8,760 hours of operation) multiplied by the gas price.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.question: What is the most accurate way to determine gas saved by replacing a high-bleed pneumatic controller, and what is the fallback?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.answer: Direct measurement of bleed emissions from both the high-bleed and low-bleed controllers is the most accurate method. If that is not possible, operators should use the manufacturers' bleed rates from product data sheets.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.evidence: Direct measurement of bleed emissions from both the high- and low-bleed controllers is the most accurate method.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.question: Why might replacing all eligible high-bleed pneumatic controllers at one time be preferable to a phased replacement?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.answer: A full replacement can be more economical because it helps minimize labor and installation costs and shutdown time.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-15.evidence: A full replacement can help minimize labor/installation costs and shutdown time.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.question: How do typical emissions from intermittent bleed pneumatic controllers compare with continuous bleed controllers?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.answer: Intermittent bleed controllers typically emit less: 323 scfd (9.15 scmd) versus 654 scfd (18.5 scmd) for continuous controllers.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.evidence: Intermittent bleed controllers typically have lower emissions than continuous controllers: 323 scfd (9.15 scmd) versus 654 scfd (18.5 scmd).

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.question: Why must Partners check that intermittent bleed pneumatic controllers are functioning properly?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.answer: Allen et al. 2014 found that malfunctioning intermittent controllers can have high emissions due to venting between actuations, so they only count as controlled if they work properly.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.evidence: Allen et al. 2014 found that intermittent controllers with malfunctions can have high emissions due to venting between actuations.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.question: What are the benefits of converting a natural gas pneumatic system to compressed instrument air?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.answer: Substituting air effectively eliminates methane emissions from control valves and pumps entirely, and adds safety benefits because a flammable substance is removed.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.evidence: By substituting air, companies are effectively eliminating methane emissions entirely from control valves and pumps, and creating additional safety benefits (because of the elimination of a flammable substance).

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.question: What does an instrument air system need to be economical for replacing gas-driven pneumatics?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.answer: It needs an accessible and reliable source of electricity and compression. Processing plants usually have the most consistent electricity, though some production, transmission and distribution facilities may too.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.evidence: Instrument air systems require an accessible and reliable source of electricity and compression to be economical and beneficial to partner companies.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.question: Which oil and gas facilities are usually best suited to instrument air systems for pneumatics?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.answer: Processing plants and facilities typically have the most consistently available electricity, which instrument air needs, although some production, transmission and distribution facilities also have reliable electricity.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-16.evidence: Typically, processing plants and facilities have the most consistently available use of electricity

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.question: What equipment makes up an instrument air system used in place of gas-driven pneumatics?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.answer: An instrument air system consists of one or more compressors, a dehydrator, a volume tank, and a power source.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.evidence: An instrument air system consists of a compressor(s), dehydrator, volume tank, and power source.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.question: What are the main costs of converting a gas-powered pneumatic system to instrument air?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.answer: The principal costs are the initial capital costs for compressors, dehydrator and volume tank, and the O&M costs of powering the compressor motor.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.evidence: The principal costs for converting a gas-powered pneumatic system to instrument air are the initial capital costs (for compressors, dehydrator, volume tank, etc.) and the O&M costs to power the compressor motor.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.question: Why can facilities with a centralized power gas system save capital costs when converting to instrument air?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.answer: Their existing gas-powered pneumatic components, such as piping, controllers and actuators, are likely compatible with instrument air, so they do not need to be replaced.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-17.evidence: existing gas-powered pneumatic components (e.g., piping, controllers, and actuators) are likely compatible with instrument air

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.question: What are the two main requirements for an instrument air system to replace gas pneumatics?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.answer: Reliable electric power, and a large enough number of pneumatic devices to justify the cost.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.evidence: The two main requirements for an instrument air system are 1) reliable electric power and 2) a large enough number of pneumatic devices to justify the cost.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.question: What rule of thumb relates utility air demand to instrument air demand when sizing an instrument air system?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.answer: Assume the maximum periodic compressed air rate for utility purposes is double the steady rate used for instrument air, so one-third of pneumatic air is for instrument air and two-thirds for utility air.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.evidence: A general rule of thumb is to assume that the maximum rate of compressed air needed periodically for utility purposes will be double the steady rate used for instrument air

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.question: How should an instrument air system be sized when the existing pneumatic gas system has no meter?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.answer: A conservative rule of thumb is one cubic foot per minute (cfm) of instrument air for each control loop, where a loop is a pneumatic controller and a control valve.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.evidence: a conservative rule of thumb for sizing air systems is one cubic foot per minute (cfm) of instrument air for each control loop

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.question: How do membrane and desiccant air dryers differ in the air-loss adjustment for instrument air sizing?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.answer: Membrane dryers lose about 17 percent of the air input, so instrument air usage is 83 percent of total compressed air supply. Desiccant dryers do not consume air and need no adjustment.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.evidence: The instrument air volume adjustment for air losses from a membrane filters air dryer is about 17 percent of the air input. As a result, the estimated volume of instrument air usage is 83 percent of the total compressed air supply

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.question: What equipment must be installed to convert gas pneumatic controls to instrument air?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.answer: An instrument air compressor, a power source for the compressor, a dehydrator or air dryer, a weatherproof enclosure and piping, and a volume tank, installed during shutdown of the related equipment.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-18.evidence: The implementation of this technology will occur during shutdown of the equipment or system related to the pneumatic device(s)

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.question: How much methane reduction can be expected from converting pneumatic controls and pumps to instrument air?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.answer: Approximately 100 percent of methane emissions from pneumatic control and pump venting.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.evidence: Companies can expect to reduce methane emissions from pneumatic controls and pump venting by approximately 100 percent after implementing this technology.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.question: What is the typical cost to convert a natural gas pneumatic control system to compressed instrument air?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.answer: A typical conversion costs approximately $45,000 to $75,000, depending on size, location and other site-specific factors.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.evidence: A typical conversion of a natural gas pneumatic control system to compressed instrument air costs approximately $45,000 to $75,000.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.question: Why do facilities commonly install two instrument air compressors?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.answer: One operates and one is on stand-by, which ensures reliability and allows maintenance and overhauls without service interruptions. Each must handle the total expected compressed air volume.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.evidence: it is common to install two compressors at a facility (one operating and one on stand-by) to ensure reliability and allow for maintenance and overhauls without service interruptions

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.question: How often are screw-type instrument air compressors overhauled and what does it cost?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.answer: Every five to six years, usually by exchanging the compressor core for a rebuilt one at about $4,000, plus $700 in labor, with a $650 salvage value.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.evidence: This normally involves exchanging the compressor core for a rebuilt compressor at a cost of approximately $4,000, with an additional $700 in labor expenses and a $650 salvage value.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.question: How is the volume tank sized for an instrument air system and what does it cost?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.answer: The rule of thumb is 1-gallon of tank capacity for each cubic foot of compressed air. Volume tanks cost about $650 to $4,000 depending on capacity and have essentially no O&M costs.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-19.evidence: the rule of thumb in determining the size of the tank is 1-gallon capacity for each cubic foot of compressed air. Volume tanks have essentially no O&M costs. A typical equipment cost range is $650 to $4,000

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.question: Which air dryers are used for small and for large instrument air systems?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.answer: Permeable membrane dryers are most common in small to medium applications. Larger systems can use multiple membrane dryers or alumina bed desiccant dryers, which are more cost-effective.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.evidence: the most common dryer used in small to medium applications is a permeable membrane dryer. Larger air systems can use multiple membrane dryers or alumina bed desiccant dryers (more costeffective).

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.question: What are typical equipment and service costs for instrument air dryers?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.answer: Air dryer equipment typically costs $2,000 to $13,100, with annual service costs of $700 to $4,300.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.evidence: Typical air dryer equipment costs are $2,000 to $13,100 and annual service costs are $700 to $4,300.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.question: Where is converting pneumatics to instrument air usually economically viable?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.answer: Because of the costs, it may only be viable for multi-well pads, large compressor stations, or large gas handling facilities.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-20.evidence: Due to the economic considerations, this option may only be viable for multi-well pads, large compressor stations, or large gas handling facilities.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.question: By how much can routing natural gas-driven pump emissions to an existing control device reduce methane emissions?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.answer: Methane emissions from natural gas-driven chemical, methanol and diaphragm pumps can be economically reduced by 95 percent if an existing control device is already available on site.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.evidence: The methane emissions from natural gas-driven chemical/methanol pumps and diaphragm pumps can be economically reduced by 95 percent if an existing control device is already available on site.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.question: What emission reductions does the OGMP estimate per pump from routing piston and diaphragm pump emissions to a control device?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.answer: Based on a 95 percent reduction, about 0.36 tpy methane and 0.10 tpy VOC per piston pump, and 3.29 tpy methane and 0.91 tpy VOC per diaphragm pump, in the production segment.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.evidence: Based on a 95 percent reduction, OGMP estimates the reduction in emissions in the production segment to be 0.36 tons per year (tpy) methane and 0.10 tpy volatile organic compounds (VOC) per piston pump and 3.29 tpy of methane and 0.91 tpy of VOC per diaphragm pump.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.question: Where can the gas from natural gas-driven pumps be routed under Mitigation Option D?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.answer: The gas can be routed to a process or to a combustor, which is often done as part of the storage tank control system.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-21.evidence: which involves routing the gas to a process or routing the gas to a combustor (often done as part of the storage tank control system)

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.question: Why do chemical injection pumps usually run on pressurized natural gas?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.answer: They are located at remote field sites that do not have reliable electrical power.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.evidence: Chemical injection pumps typically operate on pressurized natural gas because they are located at remote field sites that do not have reliable electrical power.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.question: What are the benefits of replacing pneumatic chemical injection pumps with electric pumps?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.answer: Electric chemical injection pumps can increase operational efficiency, decrease maintenance costs, and reduce emissions of methane, hazardous air pollutants and VOCs.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.evidence: the use of electric chemical injection pumps can increase operational efficiency, decreases maintenance costs, and reduce emissions of methane, hazardous air pollutants (HAPs), and VOCs

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.question: How much methanol do chemical injection pumps in gas production usually inject per day?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.answer: They are usually sized to inject 6 to 8 gallons (23 to 30 liters) of methanol a day.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.evidence: Chemical injection pumps in production are usually sized to inject 6 to 8 gallons (23 to 30 liters) of methanol a day.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.question: What injection rates and pressures can small-volume and large-volume solar chemical injection pumps handle?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.answer: Small-volume solar pumps handle about 5 gallons per day (19 liters per day) at 1,000 psig. Large-volume solar pumps inject about 38 to 100 gallons per day (144 to 380 liters per day) at 1,200 to 3,000 psig.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.evidence: Small-volume solar pumps can handle about 5 gallons per day (19 liters per day) at 1,000 psig discharge. Large-volume solar pumps typically can inject approximately 38 to 100 gallons per day (144 to 380 liters per day) at 1,200 to 3,000 psig discharge.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.question: How long do solar panels and electric motors last in solar chemical injection pump systems?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.answer: Solar panels can last up to 15 years, and electric motors in continuous use last approximately five years.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-22.evidence: Solar panels can last up to 15 years, and electric motors in continuous use have a lifespan of approximately five years.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.question: What methane reduction is expected from replacing gas-assisted pumps with solar-powered electric pumps?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.answer: A 100 percent reduction in methane emissions associated with pump venting.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.evidence: Companies can expect to achieve a 100 percent reduction in methane emissions associated with pump venting after replacing a gas-assisted system with solar power electricity.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.question: What do solar-charged electric chemical injection pumps cost to buy and install?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.answer: They cost about $2,000 per pump, with an installation cost of approximately $2,000 and no training costs.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.evidence: solar-charged electric pumps cost about $2,000 per pump. The installation cost is approximately $2,000 and no training costs for operating electric pumps are necessary.

TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.question: What gas savings and payback can be expected from replacing a pneumatic chemical injection pump with a solar pump?
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.answer: Gas savings are typically 200 Mcf (5.7 Mcm) per pump, worth $600 a year at $3 per Mcf, giving a payback of three to four years per pump.
TGD1-Pneumatic-controls-and-pumps-23.evidence: Gas savings are typically 200 Mcf (5.7 Mcm) per pump, and at $3 per Mcf, the value saved is $600 annually.
